analysis.one_liner: Requires EPA to set water pollution limits for PFAS 'forever chemicals' across eight industries.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it died in the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: PFAS are long-lasting 'forever chemicals' used in manufacturing that end up in rivers and drinking water. The bill would have forced the EPA to set legal limits on how much PFAS industrial plants can discharge — covering plastics and chemical makers, electroplating, metal finishing, textile mills, landfills, tanneries, paint and plastics plants — with deadlines of 2025 through 2027. It would have also required immediate monitoring of PFAS discharges, standardized the official EPA test method for detecting PFAS, and given wastewater treatment plants $200 million a year in grants to filter out PFAS and track where it comes from.
analysis.who_benefits: People who drink water drawn from rivers and lakes downstream of industrial plants, since PFAS have been linked to health harms and persist in the body and environment for years. Municipal wastewater utilities also gain: the bill authorizes $200 million a year for fiscal 2024-2028 to help publicly owned treatment works pretreat and trace PFAS entering their systems, plus $12 million a year for EPA's own rulemaking and testing work.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People who drink surface water downstream of industry

how_it_helps.text: Requires EPA to publish human health water quality criteria covering every measurable PFAS substance within three years of enactment, replacing a patchwork where no federal water quality criteria existed for most PFAS chemicals.

Sets hard deadlines for EPA to finalize discharge limits (effluent limitations guidelines) for eight industry categories: organic chemicals, plastics and synthetic fibers, electroplating, and metal finishing by June 2025; textile mills and landfills by June 2026; and leather tanning, paint formulating, and plastics molding by June 2027.

Requires monitoring of PFAS discharges starting immediately for the regulated industries, and for pulp and paper mills, airports, and electronics makers — with EPA required to decide by the end of 2025 whether to regulate those additional categories too.
Directs EPA to make Method 1633 — the lab test for detecting PFAS in water, solids, and tissue — the official federal test method by January 2025, so measurements are consistent and enforceable.

Authorizes $200 million per year through fiscal 2028 in grants to publicly owned treatment works for PFAS pretreatment programs and source tracking, recognizing that utilities receiving industrial wastewater often cannot remove PFAS on their own.

analysis.who_pays: The industries that discharge PFAS — chemical and plastics manufacturers, electroplating and metal finishing shops, textile mills, landfills, tanneries, and paint and plastics plants — would bear monitoring and treatment compliance costs, some of which could be passed to consumers through prices. Taxpayers fund the authorized $212 million per year in grants and EPA implementation. Municipal treatment plants also take on new monitoring and pretreatment obligations, though grants offset part of that.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs fall on a broad set of manufacturers, including smaller electroplating and metal finishing shops; treatment technology for PFAS is expensive, and some costs would likely show up in prices for metal-plated goods, textiles, and other products.

The bill sets fixed statutory deadlines (2025-2027) for rules that normally take years of technical and economic analysis; if EPA could not meet them, missed deadlines could invite litigation rather than cleaner water.
The $200 million a year in treatment-works grants is subject to appropriation, meaning Congress would have to actually fund it each year for the pretreatment program to work as designed.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health benefit is real: PFAS do not break down, so every year without discharge limits is another year of accumulation in water supplies, and EPA itself had identified these industries as major PFAS sources. The costs — compliance spending by polluting industries and roughly $212 million a year in authorized federal spending — are modest next to the scale of PFAS contamination cleanup, though the fixed deadlines were ambitious and the grants were not guaranteed funding. The bill was a straightforward push to speed up a regulatory process EPA had already begun but slowly.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, which never acted on it, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Gillibrand introduced the bill on April 18, 2024, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works the same day.
No other senator signed on as a cosponsor.
No further action was taken: no hearing, no committee markup, no floor vote. The bill died in committee when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The industries that discharge PFAS — chemical and plastics makers, electroplating and metal finishing shops, textile mills, landfills, tanneries, and paint and plastics plants — are better off, because no enforceable discharge limits or mandatory monitoring took effect. Municipal treatment plants also lost the chance at $200 million a year in cleanup grants.

for.name: Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand
for.role: U.S. Senator from New York; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Environment and Public Works Committee; no other senator joined as a cosponsor.

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote — letting it die at the end of the 118th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever held and no other senator cosponsored, so the partisan shape was never tested; the only action was a single Democratic sponsor's referral to a Democratic-chaired committee that never took it up.

industries.industry: Chemical, plastics, and synthetic fiber manufacturers
industries.note: Would have faced enforceable PFAS discharge limits by mid-2025 plus immediate monitoring. These plants are among the leading industrial sources of PFAS in waterways, so their cost is the public's benefit.

Facing the earliest deadline (June 2025) for discharge standards; many shops are small businesses that use PFAS in plating solutions. Avoiding the rule by letting the bill die kept those compliance costs off.
Would have been regulated by mid-2026. Textile mills are a known PFAS pathway from stain-resistant fabrics; landfills leach PFAS into water.

industries.industry: Leather tanning, paint, and plastics molding plants
industries.note: Would have faced discharge standards by mid-2027; avoided regulation when the bill died.

The bill would have imposed new monitoring and pretreatment duties but paired them with $200 million a year in grants. Many utilities receive PFAS-laden industrial wastewater they cannot treat, so limiting it at the source helps them.
Mandatory monitoring across many industries plus official promulgation of Method 1633 would have expanded demand for PFAS testing services.
